query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a controlled, nanoscale graphene interlayer at the tungsten–copper interfaces in W–Cu composites will improve the overall thermal conductivity by reducing interfacial thermal resistance, while preserving the required mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu metal matrix composite with standard tungsten–copper bonding interfaces.
generation.intervention: Introduce a uniformly distributed, few-layer graphene coating at the interfaces between the tungsten and copper phases during composite processing.
generation.conditions: Service conditions typical of heat-dissipation and fusion reactor joint applications, involving high thermal flux, mechanical loading, and exposure to irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered graphene interlayer at the W–Cu interfaces, which serves to bridge the dissimilar metallic phases, enhance interfacial bonding, and reduce phonon and electron scattering at the interface.
generation.mechanism: Graphene possesses exceptionally high intrinsic thermal conductivity. By forming a coherent, well-bonded interlayer between tungsten and copper, graphene is expected to facilitate efficient electron and phonon transport across the interface, thereby reducing thermal boundary resistance. Its strong bonding and two‐dimensional nature also help maintain mechanical integrity and can mitigate defect propagation under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified composite is predicted to exhibit an increased effective thermal conductivity (relative to a baseline W–Cu composite) without a reduction in mechanical strength or irradiation resistance. While the exact numerical improvement is uncertain, a significant relative enhancement (e.g., on the order of 15–30% or more) is anticipated, provided that the graphene layer is optimized.
generation.baseline: Conventional W–Cu composites manufactured without any interfacial graphene treatment.
generation.boundary: The benefits are contingent on achieving a uniform, optimally thin graphene layer; if the layer is too thick or discontinuous, it may not effectively reduce thermal resistance or could compromise mechanical properties. Extreme irradiation conditions beyond those typical of fusion device operations might also challenge the long-term stability of the graphene interlayer.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of thermal conductivity enhancement and long-term stability under sustained irradiation require experimental validation. Additionally, processing challenges in achieving defect-free, conformal graphene coatings may affect reproducibility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one incorporating the engineered graphene interlayer at the tungsten–copper interfaces, and one control sample fabricated by standard processing without graphene. Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling and irradiation conditions representative of fusion reactor joint applications.
measurements: Overall thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., using laser flash analysis) to compare effective heat transfer.
Mechanical tests (hardness, tensile and compressive strength) pre- and post-irradiation.
Irradiation damage assessment via TEM and/or other defect characterization methods.
Interfacial characterization via high-resolution SEM/TEM to verify graphene layer continuity post-treatment.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-enhanced composite fails to show a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity (e.g., less than about a 15% increase over the control) or if its mechanical durability or irradiation resistance is measurably worse than that of the control sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In parallel, it is well realized that graphene is one of the promising, low-dimensional materials with superior strength, modulus, and thermal conductivity, making it an attractive proposition for flexible electronics applications [,]. Recently, freestanding monolayer graphene exhibited an engineering tensile strength of ~50–60 GPa, a Young’s modulus up to ~1 TPa, and an elastic strain approach of ~6%, indicating near-ideal mechanical performance []: much higher than that of multilayer graphene nanosheets []. In addition to the intrinsic, superb mechanical properties of monolayer graphene, the heterogeneous metal–graphene interface renders much higher, critical resolved shear stress for dislocation cross-slip/nucleation in the vicinity of the grain boundaries, leading to an obvious increase in strength in Cu/graphene and Al/graphene composites [,]. Benefiting from the graphene interface, Cu/graphene and Ni/graphene composites show superior strength as much as 31% over the theoretical strengths [].
